How to read this: mean radiance is the area-weighted average night-time radiance inside the selected area (global = every pixel of the map). Lit area is the surface with radiance ≥ 1 nW·cm⁻²·sr⁻¹. Annual composites combine real growth in outdoor lighting with the switch to LEDs (the VIIRS sensor cannot see blue light well, so it can under-count LED growth), cloud/snow cover, calibration and short-term events such as fires, gas flares, conflict or power cuts. Rasters are quantised to 64 log levels at ~10 km pixels, so small changes (< ~3 %) are within the noise. Country ranking only lists countries larger than 15,000 km² with a first-period mean radiance ≥ 0.05.

    Light pollution: what it is, what it does, how to reduce it

    Definition

    Light pollution is the excessive, misdirected or unnecessary use of artificial light at night. It changes the natural darkness of the night environment and reaches far beyond the places where the lamps are installed.

    Skyglow – bright halo over townsGlare – harsh, blinding lightLight trespass – light where it is not neededClutter – confusing clusters of sources

    Satellites such as NASA’s VIIRS measure the light that escapes upward, so they show where and how fast outdoor lighting is spreading.

    Key facts

    • A 2024 global review estimates that about 80 % of the world’s population lives under light-polluted skies; the estimate is based on modeled night-sky brightness, not a current population census.
    • About one third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from home.
    • Between 2012 and 2016 Earth’s artificially lit area grew by about 2.2 % per year and its radiance by about 1.8 % per year.
    • Light that shines up or sideways instead of onto the ground is wasted energy and money.

    Consequences

    🌿 Wildlife & ecosystems

    • Sea-turtle hatchlings crawl toward street lights instead of the sea.
    • Migrating birds are attracted to lit towers and buildings, circle and collide.
    • Insects are trapped around lamps; fewer insects means less pollination and less food for bats and birds.
    • Predator–prey behaviour, breeding and plant flowering times are disturbed.

    🧠 Human health

    • Light at night suppresses melatonin and disrupts the body clock and sleep.
    • Studies link chronic exposure to sleep disorders, mood problems, obesity and some cancers (evidence is epidemiological and still being researched).
    • Glare reduces night vision, especially for older people and drivers.

    ⚡ Energy & climate

    • Wasted light burns electricity that is often generated from fossil fuels, adding CO₂ and costs.
    • Cheap, efficient LEDs can lead to more lighting overall (rebound effect) and to bluer, more disruptive light.

    🔭 Science & culture

    • Skyglow hides stars and limits astronomical observatories.
    • People lose a shared natural heritage: the dark night sky that inspired cultures worldwide.

    Methods to limit and fix it

    1 · Better lighting design

    • Useful: light only where and when it is needed.
    • Targeted: fully shielded, downward-facing fixtures with no upward light.
    • Low level: use the lowest brightness that does the job; avoid over-lighting.
    • Controlled: timers, dimming and motion sensors; switch off decorative, advertising and empty-building lights after hours.
    • Colour: warm light (≤ 3000 K, little blue); amber or red lights near turtle beaches and wildlife areas.

    2 · Policy & planning

    • Outdoor-lighting ordinances and national standards (e.g. Czech Republic, Slovenia, Chile’s protection of observatory skies).
    • City lighting master plans with brightness limits, curfews and shielding rules.
    • Dark-sky places, reserves and buffer zones around observatories, parks and wildlife habitats (e.g. the International Dark-Sky Association programme, started by Flagstaff, Arizona).
    • “Lights out” programmes for bird-migration seasons.

    3 · Everyone can help

    • Shield porch and garden lights, choose warm bulbs, add motion sensors.
    • Close curtains and switch off lights that are not needed.
    • Support local lighting rules and dark-sky events.
    • Measure and share: satellite data (this project) and citizen science such as Globe at Night.

    4 · Monitor with satellites

    • Compare annual night-light maps to see which areas keep growing and whether rules work.
    • Use the Growth analysis tab to compare any country with the global trend.

    Data & method

    Input: NASA VIIRS Day/Night Band night-time lights, quarterly composites (March, June, September, December) plus one yearly average per year, 2020–2026; slots stay empty until a map is added (band night_radiance, nW·cm⁻²·sr⁻¹), exported as GeoTIFF and resampled to a 4008 × 2004 grid (~10 km). Radiance is stored on a 64-step logarithmic scale up to 2,500. Country statistics use cos(latitude) area weighting and the country outlines from the uploaded Global_Borders GeoJSON (simplified to ≈1 km for the web). Growth = change in mean radiance between the first and last period with data; CAGR = compound annual growth rate.
    Sources: Kyba et al. 2024, Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, “Monitoring, trends and impacts of light pollution”; Falchi et al. 2016, Science Advances (“The new world atlas of artificial night sky brightness”); Kyba et al. 2017, Science Advances (“Artificially lit surface of Earth at night increasing in radiance and extent”); Hölker et al. 2010, Trends in Ecology & Evolution; DarkSky International (IDA) responsible-lighting principles.

    Edit places & layout

    Places CSV: name,lat,lon. Radiance values are always read from the NASA rasters (averaged over a small window around the point).
